text:
Imagine two people, Alice and Bob, who have never met and who can only talk through a channel that anyone can overhear, and who want to end up sharing a secret number that nobody listening in can work out. At first sight this looks impossible: if every word they say is heard by a third person, how can anything remain hidden? The answer, discovered in the 1970s, rests on a simple observation, that some calculations are easy to do forwards but fiendishly hard to undo, and public-key cryptography is the art of building a secret out of that imbalance.

Start with an everyday picture in which Alice and Bob each have a private pot of paint and there is also a large tub of yellow paint that everyone knows about and can use. Alice mixes her private colour into a bowl of the yellow and sends the resulting mixture to Bob, and Bob does the same with his own private colour and sends his mixture to Alice. Now each of them adds their own private colour to the mixture they received, so that Alice ends up with yellow plus Bob's colour plus her colour, and Bob ends up with yellow plus Alice's colour plus his colour. Those are the same three ingredients, so the final shade is identical. An eavesdropper saw only the yellow and the two mixtures, and because paint cannot be unmixed she cannot separate out the private colours, and she cannot make the final shade without one of them. The mathematics does the same job, with numbers in place of paint.

The first thing we need is a kind of arithmetic in which numbers wrap around, like the hours on a clock. On a twelve-hour clock, ten hours after eight o'clock is not eighteen but six, because you go past twelve and start again; mathematicians call this working with remainders, since eighteen divided by twelve leaves a remainder of six. We can choose any size of clock we like, so let us use one with twenty-three positions, numbered zero to twenty-two, and whenever a calculation gives an answer larger than twenty-two we divide by twenty-three and keep only the remainder. Everyone is told this size in advance; it is not a secret.

The second ingredient is repeated multiplication, which you know as powers. Five to the power of three means five times five times five, which is one hundred and twenty-five. Now do this on our clock: take the number five, which is also public, raise it to some power, then keep only the remainder after dividing by twenty-three. Five to the power of two is twenty-five, and twenty-five leaves a remainder of two, and five to the power of four is two times two, which is four. Because we can reduce at every step, even very large powers are quick to calculate.

Here is the imbalance: if I tell you the power, you can find the answer easily, but if I tell you the answer, say eight, and ask what power of five on the twenty-three-hour clock produces it, you have little choice but to try the powers one after another until one fits. On a clock this small that is no trouble, because there are only twenty-two possibilities, but the numbers can be made enormous. Real systems use a clock with hundreds of digits in its size, and raising a number to a huge power on such a clock takes a computer a fraction of a second, whereas working backwards from the answer to the power would take every computer on Earth longer than the age of the universe, as far as anyone knows. Easy to do, ruinously hard to undo: that is our paint that cannot be unmixed.

Now we can run the exchange with our small clock so you can check the sums yourself. Everyone knows the clock size, twenty-three, and the base number, five. Alice secretly picks the number six and calculates five to the power of six on the clock; five to the power of six is fifteen thousand six hundred and twenty-five, and dividing by twenty-three gives six hundred and seventy-nine with a remainder of eight, since twenty-three times six hundred and seventy-nine is fifteen thousand six hundred and seventeen. So Alice announces the number eight. Bob secretly picks fifteen and calculates five to the power of fifteen on the clock, which works out to nineteen, and he announces nineteen. These two announced numbers, eight and nineteen, are the equivalent of the mixed paints: anyone can hear them, and they are called public values, while the six and the fifteen stay private.

Now each person combines what they heard with their own secret. Alice takes Bob's nineteen and raises it to her private power of six, which is a big number but reduces on the clock to two, and Bob takes Alice's eight and raises it to his private power of fifteen, which on the clock also comes out as two. They have arrived at the same number without ever sending it, and the reason is that Alice's number was five raised to the power of six, so when Bob raises it to the power of fifteen he is really computing five raised to the power of six times fifteen, while Alice's route gives five raised to the power of fifteen times six. Multiplication does not care about order, since six times fifteen is fifteen times six, so both routes land on the same place. That is the whole trick.

The eavesdropper heard the clock size, the base five, and the two announcements eight and nineteen, and to reconstruct the secret two she would need either Alice's six or Bob's fifteen, which means undoing the power calculation. On our toy clock she could simply try every possibility and succeed in moments, which is why real systems use gigantic clocks, where that hunt is hopeless. Notice also that she cannot get anywhere by combining the two announcements directly: multiplying eight and nineteen, or adding them, does not produce the shared secret, because the secret depends on both private powers at once, and each announcement has hidden one of them.

What do Alice and Bob do with the shared number? They use it as the key for an ordinary, fast scrambling method, one in which the same key locks and unlocks the message, and such a method is excellent at protecting long messages but has an obvious weakness, which is that both sides need the key beforehand. Public-key methods solve exactly that problem, because the slow, clever mathematics is used only for a short moment at the start, to agree on a key in public, and then the quick method takes over for the actual conversation. This is what your web browser does in the fraction of a second after you visit a secure website.

There is a second family of public-key ideas that works a little differently, and it is worth a sentence because it gives the method its name. Here each person has two linked numbers, a public one, which they hand to everybody, and a private one, which never leaves their possession, and anything locked using the public number can only be unlocked with the private one. It is rather like a padlock that you leave open on a counter for anyone to snap shut, while only you hold the key, so that strangers can send you secrets by closing your padlock and nobody but you can open it again. The mathematics behind it relies on another easy-to-do, hard-to-undo task: multiplying two huge prime numbers together takes a moment, but splitting the result back into those primes is, for large enough numbers, beyond reach.

One honest caveat remains: the method keeps a secret from eavesdroppers, but it does not on its own prove who you are talking to, since someone sitting in the middle could pretend to be Bob to Alice and Alice to Bob, running two separate exchanges. Real systems add certificates and signatures to guard against this, but the central miracle stands: two strangers, speaking entirely in the open, can build a shared secret that the whole world heard being built and still cannot reproduce.
